subject: chemistry
question_text: Give the equation for the reaction of ethylene with hypochlorous acid.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.118, chapter 10 GENERAL ORGANIC CHEMISTRY, LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS question 33(b). PAGE AND NUMBER CHECKED AGAINST THE SOURCE INDEX (answer-book/sources/chaitanya_c1_2027_ch10_general_organic_chemistry.json), which records laq33 and all of its parts on printed page 118; p.119 carries question 34, the acetylene question. PRINTED QUESTION 33 IS ONE QUESTION WITH FIVE ASKS: it opens by asking for two methods of preparation of ethylene and then continues with the lettered parts (a)-(d), each asking for the equation of one reaction of ethylene. The opening ask is carded as ts_ipe_c1_goc_ethylene_preparation and the four lettered parts as four cards, so the shared number 33 is not a citation clash. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty. THE EQUATION WAS CHECKED ATOM BY ATOM: CH₂=CH₂ + HOCl → HOCH₂–CH₂Cl has C 2 = 2, H 5 = 5, O 1 = 1 and Cl 1 = 1. CONTENT CARRIED BEYOND THE PRINTED ANSWER and to be confirmed by a teacher: the preparation of hypochlorous acid by passing chlorine into cold water; the statement that the OH group is the negative part of HOCl and the chlorine the positive part, which follows from oxygen being more electronegative than chlorine; the IUPAC name 2-chloroethanol and the definition of a chlorohydrin; and the closing point that Markovnikov's rule is not needed for a symmetrical alkene. The equation itself and the common name ethylene chlorohydrin are the source's own.

insider_note: Hypochlorous acid adds as two parts, OH and Cl, one to each carbon of the double bond. The product is ethylene chlorohydrin, HOCH₂–CH₂Cl, and there is no by-product at all.

steps.label: The reagent
lines: Hypochlorous acid has the formula HOCl.
It is obtained by passing chlorine into
cold water.
It is an unsymmetrical reagent: the two
parts that add are the OH group and the
chlorine atom.
Oxygen is more electronegative than
chlorine, so the OH group is the negative
part and the chlorine the positive part.
steps.why: The answer needs the reagent broken into the two parts that will add, because that is what an addition to a double bond consumes. Which part is negative follows from the electronegativities in the O–Cl bond, and that is what settles the product when the alkene is unsymmetrical.
common_mistakes: Writing the reagent as HClO₂ or as Cl₂. Hypochlorous acid is HOCl.
Treating chlorine as the negative part. In HOCl the OH group is the negative part.
steps.memory_tip: HOCl adds in two parts: OH and Cl, one to each carbon.
steps.margin_note: Name the reagent and split it into the two parts that add.

steps.label: How the addition happens
lines: Ethylene has a carbon-carbon double bond,
and the π bond is the weaker of the two
bonds between those carbons.
Hypochlorous acid adds across it, and the
double bond becomes a single bond.
One carbon takes the chlorine atom and the
other takes the OH group.
Nothing is released, so the reaction is an
addition and not a substitution.
steps.why: An alkene reacts by addition because the π bond breaks and leaves one free bond on each carbon. Hypochlorous acid supplies exactly two parts, so each carbon takes one and no atom is left over — which is why there is no by-product to write.
common_mistakes: Writing a substitution that releases HCl. Ethylene adds the hypochlorous acid whole.
Putting both parts on the same carbon. One part goes to each carbon of the double bond.
Keeping the double bond in the product. It becomes a single bond when the addition happens.
steps.memory_tip: Cl on one carbon, OH on the other, and the double bond becomes single.
steps.margin_note: Say that the reaction is an addition across the double bond.

steps.label: The equation
lines: Atoms: 2 C, 5 H, 1 O and 1 Cl each side.
The product may also be written
ClCH₂–CH₂OH; it is the same compound.
Every atom of both reactants appears in
the single product, so there is no
by-product.
steps.why: Writing the OH and the chlorine on different carbons is the whole content of the equation. The atom count then confirms it: five hydrogen, one oxygen and one chlorine on each side, so nothing has been created or lost.
common_mistakes: Writing the product as CH₂=CHCl. That keeps the double bond; here the double bond opens.
Writing ClCH₂–CH₂Cl. That is the product with chlorine, not with hypochlorous acid.
Adding a second product to the equation. There is none.
steps.memory_tip: One reactant plus one reactant gives one product, with nothing released.
steps.margin_note: Write the OH group and the chlorine atom on different carbons.

steps.label: The product
lines: The product is ethylene chlorohydrin.
Its IUPAC name is 2-chloroethanol.
A chlorohydrin is a compound carrying a
chlorine atom and a hydroxyl group on
neighbouring carbon atoms.
Both groups are present in HOCH₂–CH₂Cl,
one on each carbon.
steps.why: Naming the product names its class as well: chlorohydrin says exactly what the structure is. The IUPAC name numbers the carbons from the OH end, so the chlorine sits on carbon 2.
common_mistakes: Naming the product ethylene glycol. Glycol carries two OH groups; here one of them is a chlorine atom.
Calling it 1-chloroethanol. The carbon carrying the OH is number 1, so the chlorine is on carbon 2.
steps.memory_tip: Chlorohydrin: one chlorine and one OH, on neighbouring carbons.
steps.margin_note: Give both names, the common one and the IUPAC one.

steps.label: Why only one product forms
lines: Ethylene is a symmetrical alkene: each
carbon of the double bond carries two
hydrogen atoms.
So it makes no difference which carbon
takes the chlorine, and only one product
is possible.
With an unsymmetrical alkene the two
carbons differ, and Markovnikov's rule
then places the OH group on the carbon
with fewer hydrogen atoms.
steps.why: A rule is only needed when the two carbons of the double bond are different. In ethylene they are identical, so a single product follows without any rule at all — and saying so shows the rule has been understood rather than forgotten.
common_mistakes: Applying Markovnikov's rule to ethylene. Both carbons are alike, so the rule makes no difference here.
Expecting a mixture of two products. Ethylene is symmetrical, so there is only one.
steps.memory_tip: Symmetrical alkene, one product; unsymmetrical alkene, use Markovnikov's rule.
steps.margin_note: Add one line saying why no rule is needed for ethylene itself.

steps.label: The overall change
lines: One molecule of ethylene and one of
hypochlorous acid give one molecule of
ethylene chlorohydrin.
The reaction is an addition across the
carbon-carbon double bond.
steps.why: The boxed line states the whole change on one line that can be read on its own: ethylene in, ethylene chlorohydrin out, the reagent named beside the arrow and no by-product. The full equation with HOCl on the left is written out in step 3.
common_mistakes: Adding a by-product to the boxed line. Every atom appears in the single product.
Leaving the double bond in the boxed product.
steps.memory_tip: Ethylene plus HOCl gives ethylene chlorohydrin, and nothing else.
steps.margin_note: Close with the overall change on one line, with the reagent named beside it.
